topic.name: Integration by Parts in Cyclic Cases

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{4x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 4e^{4x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{4x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{4x}\sin{x} - \int (\sin{x}) \left(4e^{4x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{4x}\sin{x} - 4\int e^{4x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= e^{4x}\sin{x} - 4J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{4x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{4x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 4e^{4x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{4x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{4x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x} \right)\left(4e^{4x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{4x}\cos{x} + 4\int e^{4x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{4x}\cos{x} + 4I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= e^{4x}\sin{x} - 4J\\[5pt] I &= e^{4x}\sin{x} - 4\left( -e^{4x}\cos{x} + 4I \right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{4x}\sin{x} + 4e^{4x}\cos{x} - 16I\\[5pt] 17I &= e^{4x}\sin{x} + 4e^{4x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac {e^{4x}\left(\sin{x} + 4\cos{x}\right)}{17} + C \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{3x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3e^{3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(5x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin(5x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\cos(5x)}{5}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{3x}\sin(5x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\left(-\dfrac{\cos(5x)}{5} \right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{\cos(5x)}{5} \right)\left(3e^{3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5} \int e^{3x}\cos(5x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{3x}\cos(5x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{3x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3e^{3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(5x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos(5x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(5x)}{5}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{3x}\cos(5x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\left(\dfrac{\sin(5x)}{5} \right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(5x)}{5} \right)\left(3e^{3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{3x}\sin(5x)}{5} - \dfrac{3}{5}\int e^{3x}\sin(5x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{3x}\sin(5x)}{5} - \dfrac{3}{5}I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5}J\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5}\left(\dfrac{e^{3x}\sin(5x)}{5} - \dfrac{3}{5}I\right)\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3e^{3x}\sin(5x)}{25} - \dfrac{9}{25}I\\[5pt] %\dfrac{34}{25}I & = -\dfrac{e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{5} + \dfrac{3e^{3x}\sin(5x)}{25}\\[5pt] \dfrac{34}{25}I & = \dfrac{3e^{3x}\sin(5x) - 5e^{3x}\cos(5x)}{25}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac {e^{3x}\left(3\sin(5x) - 5\cos(5x)\right)}{34} + C \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \int (\sin{x}) \left(e^{x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \int e^{x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x} \right)\left(e^{x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{x}\cos{x} + \int e^{x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{x}\cos{x} + I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} I &= e^{x}\sin{x} - J\\[5pt] I &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \left( -e^{x}\cos{x} + I \right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{x}\sin{x} + e^{x}\cos{x} - I\\[5pt] 2I &= e^{x}\sin{x} + e^{x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{e^{x}(\sin{x} + \cos{x})}{2} \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x & = \left(\dfrac{e^{x}(\sin{x} + \cos{x})}{2}\right)\Biggr|_{-\pi}^{\pi}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{\pi}(\sin(\pi) + \cos(\pi))}{2} - \dfrac{e^{-\pi}(\sin(-\pi) + \cos(-\pi))}{2}\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{e^{\pi}}{2} + \dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}(e^{-\pi} - e^{\pi}) \end{align}

example.title: Finding the Definite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{3x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u = e^{3x} \quad&\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3e^{3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin x \quad&\Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin x\, \textrm{d}x = -{\cos x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I &= \int e^{3x}\sin x\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\left(-{\cos x} \right) - \int \left(-{\cos x} \right)\left(3e^{3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -{e^{3x}\cos x} +3\int e^{3x}\cos x\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -{e^{3x}\cos x} +3J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{3x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{3x} \quad&\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} =3e^{3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos x \quad&\Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos x\, \textrm{d}x = \sin x. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J &= \int e^{3x}\cos x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\left({\sin x} \right) - \int \left({\sin x} \right)\left(3e^{3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\sin x -3\int e^{3x}\sin x\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{3x}\sin x - 3I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} I &= -{e^{3x}\cos x} + 3J \\[3pt] I&=-{e^{3x}\cos x} +3\left({e^{3x}\sin x} -3I\right)\\[3pt] I&=-{e^{3x}\cos x} +3e^{3x}\sin x -9I\\[3pt] 10I &= e^{3x}(3\sin x-\cos x) \\[3pt] I&= \dfrac{e^{3x}}{10}(3\sin x - \cos x) \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_0^{\pi} e^{3x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x &= \left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{10}(3\sin x - \cos x) \right)\Biggr|_0^{\pi}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{3\pi}}{10}(3\sin(\pi) - \cos(\pi)) - \dfrac{e^{3(0)}}{10}(3\sin(0) - \cos(0))\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{3\pi}}{10} + \dfrac{1}{10}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{10}(e^{3\pi} + 1) \end{align}

example.title: Finding the Definite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I= \displaystyle \int e^{-4x}\sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-4x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -4e^{-4x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I &= \int e^{-4x}\sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= (e^{-4x})(-\cos{x}) - \int (-\cos{x})(-4e^{-4x})\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-4x}\cos{x} - 4\int e^{-4x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-4x}\cos{x} - 4J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-4x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-4x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -4e^{-4x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J &= \int e^{-4x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= (e^{-4x})(\sin{x}) - \int (\sin{x})(-4e^{-4x})\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-4x}\sin{x} + 4I. \end{align*}

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve: \begin{align*} I &= -e^{-4x}\cos{x} - 4(e^{-4x}\sin{x} + 4I)\\[5pt] I &= -e^{-4x}\cos{x} - 4e^{-4x}\sin{x} - 16I\\[5pt] 17I &= -e^{-4x}(\cos{x} + 4\sin{x})\\[5pt] I &= -\dfrac{e^{-4x}}{17}\left(\cos{x} + 4\sin{x}\right). \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi} e^{-4x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x &= \left(-\dfrac{e^{-4x}}{17}\left(\cos{x} + 4\sin{x}\right)\right)\Biggr|_{0}^{\pi}\\[5pt] &= \left(-\dfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{17}\left(\cos(\pi) + 4\sin(\pi)\right)\right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{17}\left(\cos(0) + 4\sin(0)\right)\right)\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{17}(-1+0) + \dfrac{1}{17}(1+0)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-4\pi}}{17} + \dfrac{1}{17}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{17}\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1+e^{-4\pi}}\right). \end{align}
